summary: The Ahmadiyya movement was founded by Mirza Ghulam Ahmad (1835-1908) of Qadian, India, who claimed to be a prophet and the promised Messiah. The claim of prophethood after the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ contradicts the doctrine of khatm al-nubuwwah (finality of prophethood), which is established by the Quran (33:40) and the unanimous consensus (ijma') of the Muslim community. The Ahmadiyya are not considered Muslim by this consensus.
overview:
The Ahmadiyya movement (Arabic: al-Qadianiyyah) was founded in 1889 by Mirza Ghulam Ahmad (1835-1908) in Qadian, Punjab (then British India, now Pakistan). Mirza Ghulam Ahmad initially presented himself as a mujaddid (reformer) and then progressively claimed to be the promised Messiah (al-Masih al-Maw'ud), the Mahdi, and ultimately a prophet (nabi).

The central issue from an Islamic standpoint is the claim of prophethood after the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ. The Quran explicitly states in Surah al-Ahzab (33:40): 'Muhammad is not the father of any man among you, but he is the Messenger of Allah and the last (khatam) of the prophets.' This verse, combined with numerous authentic hadith and the unanimous consensus (ijma') of the Muslim community from the time of the Companions, establishes that no prophet can come after Muhammad ﷺ.

This doctrine — khatm al-nubuwwah (the finality of prophethood) — is considered a 'known necessity of religion' (ma'lum min al-din bi al-darura). Denying it is considered kufr by scholarly consensus. The Ahmadis' claim of a new prophet therefore places them outside Islam by this consensus.

The Ahmadiyya movement split in 1914 after Mirza Ghulam Ahmad's death into two branches:
1. Qadiani Ahmadis (the majority): hold that Mirza Ghulam Ahmad was a full law-bearing prophet
2. Lahori Ahmadis: hold that he was a mujaddid and reformer, not a prophet in the full sense. The Lahori branch is a smaller group and their status is debated.

Pakistan's constitution (Second Amendment, 1974) formally declared Ahmadis non-Muslim. Saudi Arabia and most Muslim-majority states do not recognize Ahmadis as Muslims. The Organization of Islamic Cooperation (OIC) and its member states have consistently maintained this position.

Islam.wiki covers the Ahmadiyya movement as a group outside Islam that uses Islamic terminology, consistent with the scholarly consensus on khatm al-nubuwwah. Individual Ahmadis are not declared kafir by name — the scholarly ruling applies to the doctrine, and individual cases of those acting in ignorance are left to Allah and qualified scholars.
disclaimer_note: The Ahmadiyya movement is not considered part of Islam by the scholarly consensus of Ahl us-Sunnah wal-Jama'ah. The founder Mirza Ghulam Ahmad claimed prophethood after the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ, which contradicts the Quranic verse (33:40) establishing Muhammad ﷺ as the final prophet and the unanimous ijma' of the Muslim community on this doctrine (khatm al-nubuwwah). Islam.wiki covers their history and beliefs for educational purposes. Individual members who may be unaware of these theological implications are not declared kafir; the scholarly ruling addresses the doctrine itself.
